profile.name: Competitive dance
profile.tagline: A rigorous staged sport where young performers execute diverse dance styles before judges.
profile.insight: Dancers balance a grueling year-round schedule of regional tours and national championships, pushing physical limits from ages five to eighteen.
profile.profile: Competitive dance is a widespread sport where participants perform routines in styles ranging from jazz and tap to contemporary before panels of expert judges. Independent production companies organize regional tours and national championships across the United States and Canada. Dancers typically range from ages five to eighteen, training year-round to maintain the extraordinary strength and flexibility required. Routines are categorized by age, experience, and group size, running from solos to massive productions.
profile.profile_long:
Competitive dance is a popular, widespread sport in which competitors perform dances in any of several permitted dance styles—such as open, acro, ballet, contemporary, jazz, hip-hop, lyrical, modern, musical theatre, tap, and improv—before a panel of judges, typically with professional dance experience. The competitive dance industry largely consists of independent production companies that conduct regional competitions along annual, nationwide tours. Dancers who compete at these regional competitions are students typically ranging in age from five to eighteen, attending classes at local dance studios or academies. After competing regionally, qualifying routines and studios go on to compete nationally towards the end of their season. Competitions typically begin in January and end in July or August.

Dancers must be physically fit because even short dances can be physically demanding. Dancers must continuously train to maintain and improve their technique, balance skills, strength, and flexibility. Except for holidays and short breaks during the summer, competitive dancing is typically a year-round activity: dancers attend classes during competition season to refine their competitive routines, and during the off-season to prepare for the next upcoming season. Some dancers attend summer dance intensives lasting a few weeks with rigorous schedules where days of twelve hours or more are extremely likely.

The music used in competitive dance routines is typically adapted from commercially available songs created by professional recording artists, or in the world of competitive ballet and musical theater can be performed by a live pianist or a full band. Because dance routines are subject to time limits at most competitions, original commercial music is usually edited to conform. There is no industry-wide standard for scoring, but awards are typically given in an order ranging from Bronze up to Diamond. Judges score performances based on technique, performance, costume, music, and difficulty level.

Competitions categorize performances into divisions based on age, experience, and group size—including solos, duets, trios, small groups, large groups, and lines or productions. Videography is frequently restricted to prevent copyright infringement of the choreography, while still photography is widely permitted without flash. Public awareness of the industry expanded significantly following the debut of the television show Dance Moms, which featured a competitive studio and its routines, though presenting a dramatized version of the real competitive world where studios typically attend five to ten competitions per year using the same routines throughout the season.

sections.origins_and_history: Competitive dance operates through independent production companies that conduct regional competitions along annual tours, primarily in the United States and Canada. In 2007, there were at least 150 such companies operating in this region. Academic and institutional surveys, such as a 2003 NCAA D-I study, examined the institutional sponsorship and funding of competitive dance and cheerleading teams across universities. Public visibility increased notably following the debut of the television show Dance Moms.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Competitors perform in permitted styles including open, acro, ballet, contemporary, jazz, hip-hop, lyrical, modern, musical theatre, tap, and improv. Group categories span solos, duets, trios, small groups (four to eight performers), large groups (nine to around twenty performers), and lines or productions (twenty-one or more performers). Specific footwork, counts, and movement techniques are not detailed in the sources, though dancers must possess high levels of physical fitness, strength, flexibility, and balance.
sections.music_and_instruments: Music is typically adapted from commercially available songs created by professional recording artists. In competitive ballet and musical theater, routines can also be performed by a live pianist or a full band. Because routines face strict time limits at most competitions, original commercial tracks are usually edited to conform.
sections.costume_and_setting: Competitions take place in venues across metropolitan areas during regional and national tour stops running from January through August. Judges evaluate performances based partly on costume. Competition production companies often employ professional photographers to capture still images, while video recording is frequently prohibited to protect copyrighted choreography.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The competitive season runs from January through August, with regional tours occurring from approximately January through May, followed by national competitions from June through August. Dancers compete for awards ranging from Bronze to Diamond, and have opportunities to win title positions such as Mr. and Miss Dance across petete, junior, teen, and senior age divisions.
